title: Delhi Destroys 7,000 Kg of Unhygienic Khoya at Mori Gate Ahead of Diwali
excerpt: Delhi's Food Safety Department seized and destroyed about 7,000 kg of foul-smelling khoya at Mori Gate Khoya Market on November 3, after 35 of 44 samples failed preliminary tests, as Chief Minister Rekha Gupta inspected the pre-Diwali crackdown.
body:
• Delhi's Food Safety Department seized and destroyed approximately 7,000 kg of unhygienic, foul-smelling khoya at Mori Gate Khoya Market on November 3, 2026, ahead of Diwali.
  • Officials collected 44 surveillance samples and tested them on the spot through the 'Food Safety on Wheels' mobile facility; 35 failed preliminary tests, and two more samples were sent to a laboratory.
  • Preliminary tests pointed to milk powder, vanaspati and binding substances in the suspected material — laboratory results will determine the final findings.
  • Reader check: to test khoya or paneer for starch at home, boil a small piece in water, cool it, and add 2-3 drops of tincture of iodine — a blue colour suggests added starch, according to FSSAI's DART guide; Delhi residents can report suspected adulteration on 1800-11-3921 during office hours.

Delhi's Food Safety Department seized and destroyed approximately 7,000 kg of unhygienic and foul-smelling khoya at the Mori Gate Khoya Market on Tuesday, November 3, in an operation inspected in person by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, according to the Chief Minister's Office account carried by ANI. The action came days before Diwali, which runs November 6-11 this year, when demand for khoya — the milk-solids base for barfi, gulab jamun and other festival sweets — rises sharply.

Gupta sought details from officials and ensured the suspected products did not enter the food supply chain, the CMO said.

"Ensuring that people have access to safe and quality food during the festive season is one of the government's foremost responsibilities. Those involved in food adulteration, regardless of how influential they may be, will be brought within the ambit of the law and face strict action."

— Rekha Gupta, Delhi Chief Minister, via the Chief Minister's Office

What officials found at Mori Gate

During the drive, the department collected 44 surveillance samples from the market and subjected them to preliminary on-the-spot testing through the 'Food Safety on Wheels' mobile testing facility. Thirty-five of the 44 samples failed the preliminary tests, according to the CMO.

Two additional samples were collected and sent to a laboratory for detailed examination. The preliminary tests also brought to light information relating to milk powder, vanaspati and substances used for binding in the suspected material, and samples were sent to the laboratory for further investigation into those ingredients. That distinction matters: the on-site results are preliminary screening, not a final laboratory confirmation of adulteration in every sample.

The wider drive also covered desi ghee. A report on the operation said that of 59 ghee samples examined, 19 were found unsafe and four did not meet quality standards. In separate raids on October 29 in Bhogal, Najafgarh and Shiv Vihar, officials seized 948.9 litres of ghee.

A fourth operation at the same market

This was the department's fourth operation at Mori Gate Khoya Market. As part of the action taken so far, the department destroyed 2,830 kg of khoya on September 4, 610 kg on September 8, and 520 kg on October 23, according to the CMO. With the November 3 seizure, the total quantity of khoya destroyed by the department so far has reached 10,660 kg.

Gupta congratulated the department team and directed it to continue with the same promptness. She said there was no place in Delhi for those who seek to spoil the joy of Diwali through food adulteration, and the CMO said the crackdown will continue.

What to check when buying festival sweets

FSSAI's DART (Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test) booklet, summarised in a festive food-safety guide, lists a simple starch check: boil a small piece of khoya or paneer with about 5 ml of water, let it cool, then add 2-3 drops of tincture of iodine. A blue colour suggests added starch; pure milk products should not turn blue. The guide describes these as screening checks, not laboratory proof.

The same guide advises buying from licensed shops — look for the FSSAI licence number at the counter or on the box — checking 'best before' dates, and asking when loose milk sweets were made. If you suspect adulteration, keep the food, box and bill, and complain to FSSAI on 1800-112-100 or the Food Safety Connect app. Delhi residents can also report adulteration or expired products on 1800-11-3921 during office hours, according to the Chief Minister's office.

What happens next

Laboratory reports will determine the next enforcement steps. For diaspora readers arranging Diwali sweets for family in Delhi: buy khoya and paneer from licensed, high-turnover shops, treat unusually cheap festival stock with caution, and use the helplines above if a purchase smells off or fails a home check.
